sweep_summary: hlai1239 (Hlai) is not in the catalog. The single keyword-matched bibliography item, Berlant 2008 on Grimm's law, is an Indo-European semiotics paper that Glottolog itself marks as a computerized mis-assignment from the word 'lexicons' — irrelevant, priority none.org) gives the best first-hand prominence statement — prefixal syllables pɯ/tsɯ/ɯ/kɯ are read in 轻声 (neutral, unstressed) tone before a fully toned main syllable (p. 8, fn. 1; p. 83); the book has no 重音 statement and treats Hlai as tonal and basically monosyllabic. Norquest 2016 (Brill; user-uploaded scan on archive.org) adds the historical picture: Proto-Hlai disyllables were iambic sesquisyllables with weight only on the rightmost main syllable, later monosyllabified. Lee 2026 (MDPI, could not be reached by automated download, read via proxy) lists eight Gei-dialect tones and is silent on stress. new_statements.rule_in_words: Hlai (Baoding dialect) is a tone language with essentially monosyllabic roots; the source never uses the term 重音 'stress'. Its only prominence statement is that derivational prefix syllables (pɯ-, tsɯ-, ɯ-, kɯ-) are 轻声, i.e. toneless/unstressed, with their pitch set by the following syllable, while the main (final) syllable keeps its full lexical tone. Read as a word-prosody statement: prominence falls on the toned main syllable, the presyllable is weak/atonic — a sesquisyllabic (iambic) pattern in prefixed words; otherwise no stress rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: pɯ and tsɯ take a neutral-tone pitch polar to the following syllable (high before a low tone, low before a high tone; shown by a raised vs. lowered dot in the transcription); ɯ and kɯ are simply neutral. Item 3(1) on the same page is ordinary tone sandhi of the first syllable in two-syllable sequences (tones 2/7 -> mid level, tone 1 -> mid falling), not stress. In the dialect chapter no comparable statement was found for the other four dialects (侾 Ha, 杞 Qi, 本地 Bendi, 美孚 Meifu, 加茂 Jiamao).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: prefix + root disyllables in citation form (examples are isolated words); the description is of the Baoding village variety (Ledong county), Luohuo subdialect of the Ha dialect, chosen by the authors as the representative variety. Nothing said about phrase-level accent.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Ouyang & Zheng 1980 (pp. 2-3) describe the speech of 保定 Baoding village, 抱由 Baoyou town, 乐东 Ledong county — the 罗活 Luohuo subdialect of the 侾 Ha dialect, chosen as the representative Hlai variety; in Glottolog 5.1 that is the dialect Ha [haaa1237] under Hlai [hlai1239] (the language has four dialects: Bendi bend1238, Ha haaa1237, Meifu meif1236, Qi qiii1237). Norquest 2016 calls this variety 'Lauhut'. Lee 2026 (silent on stress) describes the Qi/Gei dialect [qiii1237] of Tongshi/Wuzhishan. The quoted 轻声-prefix statement is therefore first-hand for Ha/Baoding only.

sources.citation: Norquest, Peter K. (2016 [c2015]). A Phonological Reconstruction of Proto-Hlai. Languages of Asia 13. Leiden/Boston: Brill. (Revision of the 2007 University of Arizona dissertation.)
sources.quote: As alluded to in chapter two, the PHl phonological word consisted of two types: either (a) monosyllabic or (b) disyllabic. Disyllabic words were certainly iambic, as this stress type is usually a necessary precondition in Southeast Asia for an eventual transition to a strictly monosyllabic inventory … The first hypothesis adopted here is that moraic weight became assigned exclusively to the main (rightmost) syllable, and that the first syllable in a disyllabic form lost the ability to host a mora. … I hypothesize that this loss of and subsequent lack of a mora was correlated with the steady erosion of presyllables until their eventual extinction in the Hlai daughter languages.
sources.note: Historical, not synchronic: ch. 4 (pp. 232-234) reconstructs the Pre-/Proto-Hlai phonological word as monosyllabic or disyllabic, the disyllables 'certainly iambic' sesquisyllables with moraic weight only on the rightmost main syllable; the presyllables eroded to extinction in the daughter languages (4.3.6 'Monosyllabification', p. 279). Ch. 4.2.3 (pp. 259-260) tentatively projects a PWKT stress distinction as the source of the PHl vowel-length contrast. No statement of stress placement in any modern Hlai language. sources.citation: Lee, Hui-chi (2026). From 'See' to 'If': The Grammaticalization of Visual Perception Verbs in Hlai. Languages 11(4): 64. DOI 10.3390/languages11040064.
sources.quote: Drawing on data collected from my fieldwork, Hlai is a tonal language. The tonal system comprises eight contrastive tones, transcribed as 33, 121, 55, 11, 51, 15, 55, and 13.
sources.note: Silent on stress. Appendix A (Qi/Gei dialect, Tongshi/Wuzhishan fieldwork): 'Hlai is a tonal language. The tonal system comprises eight contrastive tones, transcribed as 33, 121, 55, 11, 51, 15, 55, and 13', then consonant and vowel inventories. The strings 'stress/accent/prosod' occur nowhere in the article body (only in MDPI's journal-name list). MDPI itself could not be reached by automated download; full text obtained from the the Internet Archive snapshot of 2026-06-29.
